Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IoT Telnet/ADB brute-force scanner fan-out (Akiru propagation) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TuxBot v3 Evolution sample execution by SHA256 · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TuxBot/Akiru C2 & dropper connection (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127) · [LLM] DNS/HTTP resolution of TuxBot developer domain digikalas.online · [LLM] TuxBot bot-protocol beacon on TCP/31337 to public host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TuxBot/Akiru C2 & dropper connection (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to TuxBot v3 Evolution's confirmed command-and-control server (209.182.237.133, SSH banner SSH-2.0-CNC-Control-Server on TCP/2222) and the Keksec/Kaitori shared dropper host 185.10.68.127. Any internal host — especially a Linux/IoT device — reaching these IPs indicates active infection or beaconing. Rationale: Anchored on the two IOCs Unit 42 and The Hacker News both attribute to TuxBot: 209.182.237.133:2222 (SSH-2.0-CNC-Control-Server, first seen on Xpanse 2026-03-05) and the FlokiNET-hosted dropper 185.10.68.127 serving Kaitori v3.9 — fixed infrastructure, near-zero legitimate reason to contact. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html • https://community.gurucul.com/articles/ThreatResearch/TuxBot-v3-Evolution-Akiru-Framework-1-6-2026 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tools actively probing the C2 for banner grabs
  • Proxy/egress appliance logging a blocked-but-attempted connection (still worth reviewing)
  • Shared bulletproof host later re-IP'd to a benign service
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the initiating process/parent; confirm it is an IoT/Linux asset and whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked at egress. 2) Contain: block 209.182.237.133 and 185.10.68.127 at perimeter/DNS sinkhole, isolate the host from the network, snapshot for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (UC3), the sample hash 71dfbb… (UC2), DNS to digikalas.online (UC4), and any TCP/31337 or TCP/2222 sessions to other IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("209.182.237.133", "185.10.68.127")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("209.182.237.133", "185.10.68.127")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TuxBot v3 Evolution sample execution by SHA256 AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the known TuxBot x86_64 debug build (SHA256 71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d, submitted to VirusTotal 2026-01-20 with symbols). Direct hash match confirms the Akiru bot agent ran on an endpoint. Rationale: Uses the single confirmed sample hash from the development timeline (Jan 20, 2026 VirusTotal submission, x86_64 debug build with symbols) — a hash match is unambiguous, though production builds compiled with GCC 14.2.0 will differ, hence pairing with the behavioural UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR retro-scan re-surfacing the file in a quarantine path (not a live execution)
  • Analyst intentionally running the sample in a lab VM
  • Backup/restore replaying an old forensic image containing the file
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "Quarantine" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the event is a live process launch (not a quarantine/scan) and capture the full path, command line, and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, preserve the binary and memory for analysis. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same hash on other hosts, and pivot the confirmed host to C2 IP contact (UC1), Telnet/ADB scanning (UC3), and digikalas.online DNS (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where SHA256 == "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where SHA256 =~ "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IoT Telnet/ADB brute-force scanner fan-out (Akiru propagation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single internal host making high-fan-out outbound connections to Telnet (23/2323) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) across many distinct public IPs — the TuxBot bot agent's confirmed working infection vector using its 1,496 Telnet credential pairs plus SSH/HTTP/ADB scanners. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the Telnet scanner with 1,496 credential pairs is the one fully-working infection vector, plus the confirmed SSH/HTTP/ADB scanners; port 5555 (ADB) and 23/2323 (Telnet/Mirai-alt) fan-out from one host is a classic Mirai-lineage worming signature. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) sweeping the estate
  • IT asset-discovery / network-inventory tooling probing Telnet/ADB
  • Legitimate ADB debugging farm or CI device lab hitting many 5555 endpoints
  • Network monitoring appliance performing reachability checks
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.10.20.5") // add approved vuln-scanner / asset-discovery source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning host and whether it is an approved scanner (check source subnet against the authorized-scanner allowlist) and the initiating process. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and block outbound 23/2323/5555 at egress. 3) Hunt: on a confirmed compromise, pivot to C2 IPs (UC1), sample hash (UC2), and TCP/31337 bot protocol (UC5); review whether any scanned targets subsequently beacon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // mass Telnet/ADB scanning; bot brute-forces 1,496 cred pairs across many hosts
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceHostName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // mass Telnet/ADB scan fan-out
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=23 OR RemotePort=2323 OR RemotePort=5555)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count > 100

DNS/HTTP resolution of TuxBot developer domain digikalas.online AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS queries or HTTP connections to the TuxBot developer/operator domain digikalas.online and its subdomains (e.g. newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online), registered via Namecheap with Withheld-for-Privacy and resolving to Iran's Arvan Cloud CDN — used across the framework's build and fallback-C2 infrastructure. Rationale: digikalas.online is the operator's registered domain (Aug 6, 2025, Withheld for Privacy ehf, Arvan Cloud) and its subdomain newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online leaked in the MHDDoS Git log; a wildcard host-match catches both the leaked dev host and any fallback-C2 subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform auto-resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • Analyst manually browsing the domain during investigation
  • DNS logging appliance replaying a passive-DNS feed
  • Typosquat lookalike unrelated to the actor (verify exact domain)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR IOC-enrichment resolvers
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and initiating process; confirm the query is exactly digikalas.online (not a benign lookalike) and whether it resolved. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS, isolate the host if the query originated from an application process rather than a browser. 3) Hunt: pivot the host to C2 IP contact (UC1), sample hash (UC2), and Telnet/ADB scanning (UC3); add the resolved Arvan Cloud IP to watchlists.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "digikalas.online"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "digikalas.online"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TuxBot bot-protocol beacon on TCP/31337 to public host AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound TCP connections to port 31337 — the bot-protocol port hard-coded in the analyzed TuxBot build's encrypted C2 channel. Lower-fidelity than the IP/hash UCs because the port is operator-configurable, so scoped as a per-host beaconing hunt. Rationale: The analyzed development build set the bot protocol port to 31337 (with C2 at loopback 127.0.0.1); the port is a concrete, article-stated value but modifiable in production, so this is framed as a hunting-tier per-host beacon rather than an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy/CTF or 'elite'-port test services intentionally bound to 31337
  • Back Orifice-era honeypot or deception tooling listening on 31337
  • Custom internal application coincidentally using port 31337
  • Pentest C2 framework in an authorized engagement
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pentest-c2.exe") // exclude sanctioned red-team tooling by process name
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, initiating process, and destination IP; check whether the destination overlaps the known C2 IPs (UC1) or resolves from digikalas.online (UC4). 2) Contain: if the process is not an approved application, isolate the host and block 31337 egress. 3) Hunt: correlate with Telnet/ADB scanning (UC3) and the sample hash (UC2) on the same host; profile beacon regularity to confirm C2 rather than one-off.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 31337
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Targets = make_set(RemoteIP, 10) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Count desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 31337
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName
| order by Count desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("209.182.237.133", "185.10.68.127") or RemoteUrl has_any ("digikalas.online", "newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task maintaining reverse SSH-over-RDP tunnel AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a scheduled task literally named 'Apple Sync' that OkoBot's SSH bot registers to re-establish a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding the local RDP port every hour. This is a unique, framework-specific persistence + C2-maintenance artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim task name 'Apple Sync' (article code block + corroborated by Securelist/TheHackerNews); a fixed, non-generic string with essentially no legitimate use, making it a high-fidelity alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Apple/iTunes/iCloud sync helper task (Apple's tasks use different names such as 'AppleSoftwareUpdate' — verify exact string and command action)
  • MDM/RMM tooling deploying a task that coincidentally contains the words Apple Sync
  • Analyst red-team emulating OkoBot in an authorized exercise
  • Backup software creating an hourly task with an ssh action
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppleSoftwareUpdate","MobileDeviceService") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","AppleSoftwareUpdate.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (schtasks /query /tn "Apple Sync" /xml) and confirm it launches ssh.exe with -R remote port forwarding to an external host. 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, kill the ssh.exe tunnel process, and block the destination IP at the firewall; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe, a patched termsrv.dll, and additions to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Apple Sync"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","ssh","-R")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Apple Sync"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot termsrv.dll patch for concurrent multi-session RDP AIInstallation High
Detects replacement/modification of the system library C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll by a process other than Windows servicing components. OkoBot swaps in a patched termsrv.dll to permit multiple concurrent RDP sessions on the victim. Rationale: System32\termsrv.dll is only legitimately written by Windows servicing (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker); any other writer patching it is the exact multi-RDP evasion Securelist describes and independently reported against the same TTP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://www.cryptika.com/cloud-atlas-apt-group-modifies-termsrv-dll-to-enable-multiple-rdp-sessions-on-victim-hosts/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/feature update replacing termsrv.dll via TrustedInstaller (excluded by the process filter)
  • Legitimate 3rd-party 'RDP Wrapper' installs by IT for multi-session labs
  • Disk imaging/restore tools rewriting system files during recovery
  • Security product self-protection rollback restoring the file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\WinSxS\" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "drvinst.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the on-disk termsrv.dll hash/version against the OS build's Microsoft-signed baseline and confirm the writing process is not a servicing component. 2) Contain: restore the original signed termsrv.dll (sfc /scannow or WinSxS restore), disable RDP if not required, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Apple Sync' task, new members of 'Remote Desktop Users', inbound-RDP firewall rules, and HDUtil.exe on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MsMpEng.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername

OkoBot HDUtil launcher execution from %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo with 'target' deploy command AIInstallation High
Detects the VMProtect-packed OkoBot launcher HDUtil.exe running from %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo, or any child it spawns via its 'target'/'nouac'/'noattach' module-deployment commands. HDUtil is the framework's payload dispatcher. Rationale: HDUtil.exe and its fixed install path %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo\HDUtil.exe are named IOCs (Securelist + TheHackerNews); the binary name and directory have no legitimate software counterpart, and pivoting on its children surfaces every deployed module. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1480
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign in-house utility coincidentally named HDUtil.exe (verify signer and path — legitimate ones will not sit in %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo)
  • Hard-drive vendor diagnostic tools using a similar name (validate publisher signature)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Renamed/allow-listed admin tool in the HDVideo path (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is unsigned/VMProtect-packed and located under %PROGRAMDATA%\HDVideo; capture its command line for 'target'/'nouac' arguments and check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, quarantine HDUtil.exe and any child payloads (e.g. extl.exe), and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all children of HDUtil across the fleet and pivot to the C2 domain moonsand[.]store and the 'Apple Sync' task.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
    or FolderPath has @"\HDVideo\"
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\HDVideo\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "HDUtil.exe"
    or ParentProcessName has "HDUtil.exe"
    or TargetProcessName has @"\HDVideo\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot UAC bypass via auto-elevated msconfig.exe spawning child process AIExploitation Medium
Detects the OkoBot 'nouac' technique in which the auto-elevated, Microsoft-signed msconfig.exe is abused (via a Windows RPC/COM elevation trick) to launch a payload at High integrity. Legitimate msconfig rarely spawns child processes. Rationale: The article names msconfig.exe as the auto-elevated binary abused for stealthy UAC bypass (Project Zero 2019 technique); msconfig spawning any non-conhost child at High integrity is an anomalous, article-specific privesc signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1548.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually opening msconfig and clicking 'Launch' on a startup/service item
  • msconfig used to relaunch services.msc or other MMC snap-ins during troubleshooting
  • Software installers that shell out to msconfig for boot configuration
  • Help-desk remote sessions running system configuration utilities
Suppression filter
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("High","System") and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process (image path, signer, integrity level) and confirm it is unsigned/from a suspicious path rather than an interactive admin action. 2) Contain: kill the elevated child, quarantine its image, and isolate if the child matches OkoBot modules (extl.exe, HDUtil.exe). 3) Hunt: correlate with a preceding HDUtil 'target nouac' command line and Defender-notification-disabling registry writes on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msconfig.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "msconfig.exe"
| where TargetProcessName !has "conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessIntegrityLevel, ParentProcessCommandLine

OkoBot extl.exe browser-extension injector deploying Rilide Chromium stealer AIInstallation High
Detects execution of OkoBot's extl.exe injector — deployed via 'HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' — which sideloads the Rilide Chromium stealer to harvest crypto-wallet browser extension data. Targets the specific injector binary and its HDUtil parentage. Rationale: extl.exe is the named browser-extension injector and the 'HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' command is quoted verbatim; both are unique OkoBot strings tied to the Rilide Chromium wallet-extension stealer confirmed by TheHackerNews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated internal tool named extl.exe (verify signer/path)
  • Legitimate enterprise browser-extension management deploying policies
  • Chromium developer tooling loading unpacked extensions during testing
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Google")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm extl.exe is unsigned and, if present, inspect the browser's Local Extension Settings / Extensions folders for unauthorized Rilide artifacts. 2) Contain: kill extl.exe, remove the injected extension, quarantine binaries, and force-reset affected browser profiles. 3) Hunt: check for crypto-wallet access (Ledger/Trezor/Exodus/MetaMask) and exfil to moonsand[.]store from the host.

| where FileName =~ "extl.exe"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "extl")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "extl.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,

          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

    or (ParentProcessName has "HDUtil.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "extl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot C2 beacon to moonsand[.]store / reverse SSH tunnel egress AICommand & Control High
Detects endpoint connections resolving or connecting to the OkoBot C2 domain moonsand[.]store, or ssh.exe establishing an outbound reverse tunnel (-R remote forwarding) to a public host — the framework's SFTP module-delivery and RDP-forwarding channel. Rationale: moonsand[.]store is a discrete C2 IOC surfaced by TheHackerNews's OkoBot write-up; combined with ssh.exe reverse-tunnel (-R) egress it covers both the DNS/HTTP and SSH channels the framework uses for SFTP module delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using ssh.exe -R for authorized reverse tunneling (verify the .ssh\go.bat and destination)
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or researcher resolving moonsand[.]store for analysis
  • Security proxy/DNS-inspection appliance pre-resolving flagged domains
  • Web-content scanner crawling the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that resolved moonsand[.]store or ran ssh.exe -R and confirm the destination is attacker-controlled (check %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\go.bat). 2) Contain: block moonsand[.]store and the SSH destination IP at egress, kill the ssh.exe tunnel, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for moonsand[.]store, and on hits pivot to HDUtil.exe, the 'Apple Sync' task, and patched termsrv.dll.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "moonsand.store"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "moonsand.store"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

OkoBot RDP enablement: user added to 'Remote Desktop Users' + inbound-RDP firewall rule AIInstallation Medium
Detects the OkoBot SSH bot's graphical-session setup: adding a local account to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, opening inbound RDP via netsh firewall, and/or clearing fDenyTSConnections — the precursor to its multi-session RDP access. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit back-connection steps (open inbound-RDP firewall ports, add a user to 'Remote Desktop Users'); grouping the three commands raises fidelity above any single admin action. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1562.004 T1136.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT enabling RDP on a workstation for legitimate remote support
  • GPO/Intune configuration scripts opening RDP firewall rules
  • Sysadmin adding a helpdesk account to Remote Desktop Users
  • Server provisioning automation clearing fDenyTSConnections
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "MDM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/account and whether the change was ticketed IT activity or driven by an unknown parent (e.g. ssh.exe, HDUtil.exe). 2) Contain: revert the group membership and firewall rule, re-enable fDenyTSConnections, and isolate if unauthorized. 3) Hunt: correlate with the 'Apple Sync' task, patched termsrv.dll, and new local accounts; check for subsequent inbound RDP logons (LogonType 10).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and ProcessCommandLine has "/add")
    or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("3389","Remote Desktop","RemoteDesktop"))
    or ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and CommandLine has "/add")
    or (NewProcessName has "netsh.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("3389","Remote Desktop","RemoteDesktop"))
    or CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

OkoBot SeedHunter memory injection into cryptocurrency wallet applications AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts remote-thread/process-memory injection into desktop crypto-wallet apps (Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Exodus, Tonkeeper) — the mechanism OkoBot's SeedHunter/OkoSpyware modules use to overlay seed-phrase phishing and capture recovery phrases from wallet windows. Rationale: TheHackerNews confirms SeedHunter injects seed-phrase phishing into Ledger and Trezor apps; hunting cross-process injection into these named wallet binaries targets the collection mechanism directly. Sentinel left empty because the canonical tenant schema lacks an API-call/injection table (DeviceEvents is not onboarded); use Defender/Falcon or Sysmon EID 8/10. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1055 T1113
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate security/EDR agents reading wallet-app memory for scanning
  • Wallet auto-updaters or crash-reporters accessing their own process (excluded by self-filter)
  • Accessibility/overlay tools (screen readers, password managers) hooking wallet windows
  • Debuggers used by a wallet developer on the endpoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","CrowdStrike, Inc.") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the injector process (path, signer) accessing the wallet app; confirm it is not the wallet's own updater or an EDR agent. 2) Contain: kill the injector, quarantine its binary, and advise the user their seed phrase may be compromised — move funds from a clean device. 3) Hunt: link to HDUtil.exe/extl.exe, OkoSpyware/MC Keylogger artifacts, and exfil to moonsand[.]store on the host and any wallets accessed from it.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall","QueueUserApcRemoteApiCall")
| where FileName in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          TargetApp = FileName,
          Injector = InitiatingProcessFileName, InjectorPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InjectorCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall","QueueUserApcRemoteApiCall")
| where FileName in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Ledger Live.exe","Trezor Suite.exe","Exodus.exe","Tonkeeper.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType,
          TargetApp = FileName,
          Injector = InitiatingProcessFileName, InjectorPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InjectorCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma sync.js loader dropped to OS-specific path by node and executed · [LLM] Miasma persistence via Windows Run key or startup written by node/npm process · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Miasma botnet C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Install of compromised @asyncapi npm package versions (generator/helpers/components/specs) AIDelivery High
Hunts for developer or CI hosts installing the specific poisoned @asyncapi package versions published on 2026-07-14 that carry the Miasma dropper. Grounded on the exact package@version strings from the article, so it flags exposure regardless of whether the module was ever require()d. Rationale: Uses the five exact compromised package@version strings named in the article and confirmed by Socket/StepSecurity/OX Security. These versions were unpublished, so any residual reference is high-fidelity exposure evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A remediation/IR engineer intentionally installing the pinned bad version in an isolated lab to reverse it
  • An internal mirror serving a cached copy that still lists the old version in a lockfile audit command
  • Security scanner (e.g. Socket/Snyk CLI) echoing the package@version string in its own command line while auditing
  • A developer typing the version in a `npm view @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1` diagnostic command
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm view" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "audit"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user ran the install and whether it was a build/CI agent or a dev laptop; check DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child spawned shortly after. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate any credentials reachable from it (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS keys, SSH keys, browser sessions) and remove the package from the affected lockfile/registry cache. 3) Hunt: pivot to IPFS gateway fetches of CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9, sync.js file drops, and outbound connections to 85.137.53.71.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawns detached background node fetching Miasma stage-2 from IPFS gatewa AIDelivery High
Hunts the require()-time dropper behaviour where a node/npm process launches a detached child node that pulls the encrypted stage-2 (sync.js) from the IPFS gateway. Anchored on the article's IPFS CID and gateway path rather than a generic node-spawns-node pattern. Rationale: Combines the article's parent-child chain (module load -> detached node) with the exact IPFS CID/gateway path and sync.js loader name, giving a high-fidelity delivery-stage detection distinct from generic node execution. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit IPFS-based dev tool (e.g. js-ipfs/Helia) fetching content via ipfs.io through node
  • A frontend project genuinely named sync.js being launched with node during a build
  • A developer manually curl-ing an IPFS gateway inside an npm run script for testing
  • Package tarball integrity tooling referencing an ipfs.io mirror
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9" or ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child node command line and the parent lockfile/module path; confirm the CID matches QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9. 2) Contain: kill the detached node process tree, isolate the host, and block the IPFS gateway CID at proxy. 3) Hunt: look for sync.js written to temp/appdata, registry Run-key persistence written by node, and beacons to 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IPFS gateway fetch of Miasma stage-2 CID (ipfs.io/ipfs/QmQobZSp...) AIDelivery High
Network-layer detection for a host retrieving the encrypted second stage from the exact IPFS CID hosted on ipfs.io. Pivots on the CID string in the URL, which uniquely identifies this campaign's payload regardless of the fetching process. Rationale: The IPFS CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 in the download URL is a unique campaign IOC confirmed across Socket, SafeDep and Datadog; the URL-path match is near-zero FP. DNS-only fallback (ipfs.io + node) is used where proxy telemetry is absent. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the public ipfs.io gateway by a decentralized-app developer
  • A CI job resolving ipfs.io for an unrelated, benign CID (only the DNS fallback clause, not the CID clause)
  • Security researcher fetching the CID for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • Corporate proxy prefetch/cache warming ipfs.io
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL contained the exact CID (true positive) vs a generic ipfs.io hit (needs enrichment); identify the fetching process. 2) Contain: block the CID/gateway at web proxy and isolate the host if the CID matched. 3) Hunt: correlate to the node parent chain, sync.js drop, persistence writes, and 85.137.53.71 beaconing on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
   or (RemoteUrl has "ipfs.io" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9" or Url has "ipfs.io/ipfs"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent

Miasma sync.js loader dropped to OS-specific path by node and executed AIInstallation Medium
Detects the encrypted stage-2 JavaScript loader 'sync.js' being written by a node/npm process to a staging path, the precursor to Miasma tasking-framework execution. Scoped to node-parented writes plus temp/appdata/hidden-dir staging seen in the campaign. Rationale: sync.js is the article's named stage-2 loader; pairing the exact filename with a node/npm writer and the campaign's staging locations (temp/appdata/.config/.cache/node_modules per Datadog & CybersecurityNews) keeps FPs on the common filename manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browsersync/webpack-dev-server writing a sync.js helper during a build
  • A project that legitimately ships a module named sync.js into node_modules
  • Editor autosave dropping sync.js into an AppData temp workspace
  • Test frameworks generating sync.js fixtures in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/.miasma", "mesa_shader_cache") or SHA256 in ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1","082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab","bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare to the article SHA256 set; inspect the writing node command line and parent package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate developer credentials if execution followed the write. 3) Hunt: check for immediate outbound to ipfs.io CID or 85.137.53.71, plus systemd/launchd/Run-key persistence created by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\node_modules\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "/.config/", "/.cache/", "/tmp/", "node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
