FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262: parenthesis-bypass SQLi in REST API filter parameter AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-45262 exploit where the /api/3 filter[] key contains both '(' and ')' to bypass Where::sqlColumn identifier escaping and inject a UNION SELECT. Targets the specific FacturaScripts REST routes (/api/3/clientes, /api/3/attachedfiles) with a filter key carrying parentheses plus SQL keywords. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-45262 sink prerequisites from the article: the /api/3/clientes and /api/3/attachedfiles routes, a filter[] key that must contain both '(' and ')' to reach the un-escaped branch of Where::sqlColumn, and the UNION SELECT ... FROM users WHERE(nick='admin')-- payload. url_decode() normalises the %28/%29/%20 encoding the article shows. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/ • https://github.com/NeoRazorX/facturascripts/security/advisories/GHSA-g6w2-q45f-xrp4
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate API clients using expression columns like filter[lower(nombre)] or filter[LOWER(cifnif)] which also contain parentheses (article notes the branch exists to support LOWER()/UPPER() columns)
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, sqlmap, Acunetix) probing the tenant during authorised pentests
  • Analysts pasting an encoded PoC URL into a browser against a staging host
  • Web-app firewalls that rewrite/annotate query strings and inject SQL-looking tokens into the logged URL
Suppression filter
| where not(DecodedUrl matches regex @"filter\[(lower|upper)\([a-z0-9_]+\)\]") // drop legitimate expression-column filters
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DecodedUrl and SrcIpAddr; confirm the filter[] key literally contains parentheses + a SQL verb (UNION/SELECT/FROM users) rather than a legitimate LOWER()/UPPER() column. Check HttpStatusCode==200 and HttpResponseBodyBytes for a large body indicating a successful dump. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF, revoke every FacturaScripts ApiKey (attacker likely captured admin logkey/password hash), force admin password reset, and confirm FacturaScripts is patched past the fixed release. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent 200s to /AdminPlugins, /AdminHome and other /Admin* routes (leaked logkey reuse), and search for repeated filter[] parenthesis payloads across all /api/3/* resources.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/"
| where DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where DecodedUrl contains "(" and DecodedUrl contains ")"     // Where::sqlColumn parenthesis-exemption trigger
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "from users", "information_schema", "-- ")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, DstHostname, Url, DecodedUrl, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262: admin takeover via leaked logkey reuse to /AdminPlugins AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a source IP that sent the parenthesis-bypass SQLi against /api/3 with a subsequent HTTP 200 to admin routes (/AdminPlugins, /AdminHome). In the PoC the SQLi leaked the admin logkey cookie, which was replayed to reach the admin plugin-management UI — this is the account-takeover step. Rationale: Encodes the article's end-to-end takeover: the leaked logkey cookie was injected into a fresh jar and 'GET /AdminPlugins returned 200 with the admin plugin management UI.' Correlating a 200 to /AdminPlugins or /AdminHome from the same SrcIp that submitted the filter[] parenthesis SQLi is high-fidelity because normal API clients never touch the admin UI. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/
ATT&CKT1078 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine administrator who both uses the API and manages plugins from the same egress IP (small single-tenant deployments)
  • Shared corporate NAT/proxy where API traffic and admin browsing exit the same public IP
  • Vulnerability scanner that crawls both /api/3 and /Admin* routes in one authorised assessment
  • Load balancer health checks or synthetic monitors hitting admin endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SqliFirst timestamp precedes the /AdminPlugins 200, and that the SrcIp's SQLi query carried a real UNION/nick= payload. Compare the SrcIp against the admin's known office/VPN ranges. 2) Contain: invalidate all active FacturaScripts sessions (rotate logkey/secret), force admin credential reset, disable/rotate every ApiKey, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: enumerate other /Admin* routes hit by the SrcIp (plugin installs, user creation), review FacturaScripts audit/plugin directories for newly added plugins or webshells, and check for outbound connections from the FacturaScripts host.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SqliSources = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
    | where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/" and DecodedUrl contains "filter"
    | where DecodedUrl contains "(" and DecodedUrl contains ")"
    | where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "from users", "nick=")
    | summarize SqliFirst = min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("/adminplugins", "/adminhome")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| join kind=inner SqliSources on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated >= SqliFirst        // admin access AFTER the injection
| project TimeGenerated, SqliFirst, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts /api/3/clientes response-size anomaly (SQLi data dump) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags /api/3/clientes responses whose body is far larger than the endpoint's baseline while the request carries a filter[] parameter — the signature of a UNION SELECT dumping the users table (password hash + logkey) through the clientes serialiser. Distinct pivot from the request-signature UC: it catches a successful exfil even if the payload encoding evaded the request-side rule. Rationale: The article states the injected UNION mirrors the clientes table's 32 columns so the leaked admin hash/logkey are returned inside the JSON 'cifnif' key — a successful dump inflates the response body well above a normal clientes read. Pairing the size anomaly with the presence of a filter[] parameter keeps it article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/
ATT&CKT1190 T1005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bulk exports / large limit= page reads of the clientes list
  • Reporting or ETL integrations that pull the full customer table
  • First run after a data import when clientes row count spikes
  • A tenant with genuinely large customer records (long notes/addresses) skewing the P95
Suppression filter
| where not(DecodedUrl contains "limit=" and not(DecodedUrl contains "(")) // keep injection-shaped filters, drop plain large paged reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request's filter[] value for parenthesis + UNION/SELECT tokens and the SrcIp; a legitimate bulk read will use limit=/offset= not a parenthesised filter key. 2) Contain: if the filter carries injection syntax, treat as confirmed dump — rotate admin credentials, all ApiKeys and the app secret, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: review the same SrcIp for /api/3 requests against other resources (proveedores, users, attachedfiles) and for subsequent admin-UI access via leaked logkey.
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
    | where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
    | summarize P95 = percentile(HttpResponseBodyBytes, 95);
let P95Bytes = toscalar(Baseline | project P95);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
| where DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > (P95Bytes * 3)    // 3x the 95th-percentile normal clientes response body
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpResponseBodyBytes, P95Bytes, HttpStatusCode
| order by HttpResponseBodyBytes desc

FacturaScripts filter[] SQLi obfuscation: multiple distinct encodings from one source AIExploitation Medium
Detects a single source submitting several distinct encodings of a filter[] SQL-injection payload (mixed %28/%29, %20, /**/, case variation) to the /api/3 API within a short window — WAF-evasion / payload-tuning behaviour against the CVE-2026-45262 parenthesis bypass. Aggregation pivot on source, complementary to the single-request signature rule. Rationale: The article's PoC mixes literal syntax with %20/%28/%5B encoding and comment tokens (-- ); an attacker tuning the parenthesis bypass against a WAF will emit multiple distinct encodings of the same logical filter payload. Keying dcount on the raw (encoded) filter token surfaces that variation while the decoded-token filter keeps it scoped to SQLi attempts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5qmh-x653-g8qj
ATT&CKT1027 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised DAST/sqlmap runs which by design mutate payload encodings rapidly
  • A buggy client retrying the same filter with slightly different URL-encoding libraries
  • Fuzzing during QA of a new API integration
  • Browser vs. mobile-app clients double-encoding the same legitimate filter differently
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the make_set of FilterPayloads for the SrcIp — confirm they are encoding variants of a UNION/SELECT/parenthesis payload rather than distinct legitimate filters. 2) Contain: block the SrcIp at the WAF and add a virtual-patch rule rejecting /api/3 filter[] keys containing '(' + ')' with SQL verbs; confirm FacturaScripts is patched. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the variants returned HTTP 200 with an inflated body (successful bypass) and pivot the SrcIp to the admin-takeover and response-size detections.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/" and DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "(", "sleep(", "information_schema")
| extend FilterPayload = extract(@"filter[^&]*", 0, tolower(Url))    // raw (still-encoded) filter token so different encodings stay distinct
| summarize DistinctPayloads = dcount(FilterPayload), Payloads = make_set(FilterPayload, 10), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctPayloads > 3        // >3 distinct filter[] encodings in 5 min = WAF-evasion / payload tuning
| order by DistinctPayloads desc

LabubaRAT nvidia-sysruntime.exe launch with runtime C2 config in command line AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the LabubaRAT loader binary 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' that impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit and takes its C2 server (pipicka.xyz) and polling interval as launch arguments — or as a single Base64-encoded argument. Article-specific because the same compiled binary is re-tasked per campaign purely via command line. Rationale: Pivots on the exact named loader 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' plus the hard IOC pipicka.xyz appearing in the launch arguments (article states C2 + polling interval are passed at runtime, optionally Base64-encoded). Cross-checked against SC Media and the KSEC intel forum. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate NVIDIA container runtime tooling that ships a similarly named binary (validate signer + folder path)
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored corporate host
  • Red-team engagement replaying LabubaRAT TTPs
  • EDR sample-submission automation renaming test binaries to 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe'
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any Base64 argument to recover the C2 host + polling interval; confirm the binary is NOT signed by NVIDIA and not under \Program Files\NVIDIA. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host and kill/quarantine nvidia-sysruntime.exe and its SQLite config DB. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/filename org-wide, look for pipicka.xyz DNS/HTTPS beacons, Run-key persistence, and the AV-enumeration behavior on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "nvidia-sysruntime"
| extend C2Config = case(ProcessCommandLine has "pipicka.xyz","pipicka.xyz", ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}","base64_arg","none")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, C2Config, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

| extend C2Config = case(CommandLine has "pipicka.xyz","pipicka.xyz", CommandLine matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}","base64_arg","none")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, C2Config, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LabubaRAT C2 beacon to pipicka.xyz (HTTPS / DNS tunneling) from NVIDIA-impersonating host AICommand & Control High
Hunts network and DNS traffic to the LabubaRAT C2 domain pipicka.xyz, including data-carrying subdomains characteristic of the implant's DNS-tunneling communication path. Article-specific because pipicka.xyz is the confirmed default C2 and DNS tunneling is one of its three named channels (HTTPS, WebView2, DNS). Rationale: pipicka.xyz is the confirmed hard C2 IOC; the subdomain-length logic surfaces the DNS-tunneling channel the article explicitly names. Corroborated by SC Media. Sentinel query rewritten to use DnsEvents.Name/ClientIP (not the invalid IPAddresses column) and ImDnsActivity.DnsQuery. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/DNS-sinkhole platforms actively resolving pipicka.xyz for enrichment
  • Security appliances pre-resolving IOC domains from a feed
  • Analyst manually querying the domain during investigation from a corporate workstation
  • Passive-DNS / URL-detonation sandbox traffic
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","ti-","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ContextProcess/InitiatingProcess behind the query — confirm it is nvidia-sysruntime.exe or another non-NVIDIA binary; inspect subdomain entropy/length for tunneled data. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block pipicka.xyz at the resolver and firewall, isolate the querying host. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts resolving *.pipicka.xyz in 30d, correlate with nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and Run-key persistence; capture beaconing interval to recover the polling-interval config.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "pipicka.xyz" or RemoteUrl contains ".pipicka.xyz"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".pipicka.xyz")[0])
| extend TunnelingSuspected = iff(strlen(Subdomain) > 30, "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, TunnelingSuspected
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=DvcHostname, Query=DnsQuery, Src2="", Source=EventProduct),
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=ClientIP, Host=Computer, Query=Name, Src2=QueryType, Source="MicrosoftDNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationDnsDomain has "pipicka.xyz" or RequestURL has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Query=coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), Src2=DestinationIP, Source=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-branded process spawns shell / LOLBin (LabubaRAT operator tasking) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any process whose image name starts with 'nvidia' spawning cmd/powershell/script hosts/LOLBins — legitimate NVIDIA software does not launch interactive shells. Captures LabubaRAT's command-execution, PowerShell-execution and JavaScript-execution operator capabilities running under its NVIDIA masquerade. Rationale: Article states LabubaRAT masquerades as NVIDIA software and supports command/PowerShell/JavaScript execution; genuine NVIDIA binaries never parent interactive shells, making the nvidia-parent → shell-child pair high-signal for the malware's operator tasking. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GeForce Experience / NVIDIA installer legitimately shelling out to run driver-cleanup scripts
  • NVIDIA telemetry or crash-reporter invoking rundll32 during driver install
  • IT deployment tooling wrapping a renamed nvidia*.exe launcher
  • Third-party 'nvidia'-prefixed OEM utility spawning cmd for a config task
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the parent nvidia*.exe signer and path — genuine NVIDIA lives under \Program Files\NVIDIA and is Authenticode-signed by NVIDIA; inspect the child command line for discovery/download activity. 2) Contain: if parent is unsigned/misplaced, isolate host and quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: check the same host for pipicka.xyz beacons, Run-key persistence, and AV/browser enumeration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName contains "\\nvidia" and ParentProcessName endswith ".exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-named executable without valid NVIDIA code signature AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of binaries whose filename starts with 'nvidia' but whose embedded company/signer is not NVIDIA — the core file-level masquerade LabubaRAT relies on (impersonating NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit). Flags nvidia-sysruntime.exe and any re-branded variant that fails to chain to NVIDIA's trusted publisher. Rationale: Directly operationalizes the article's 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise: Defender's ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName lets us flag nvidia-named binaries whose signer isn't NVIDIA. Sentinel left blank because SecurityEvent 4688 carries no signer/company field to express the mismatch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OEM/laptop-vendor NVIDIA helper utilities signed under the OEM's name rather than NVIDIA
  • Portable NVIDIA tools run from a user Downloads folder before install
  • Older NVIDIA components with stripped/blank version metadata
  • Internal software-packaging wrappers that re-sign an nvidia launcher with a corporate cert
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Dell","HP","Lenovo","ASUS","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: compute the SHA256 and check reputation; confirm the file is the LabubaRAT loader vs a legitimately OEM-signed helper. 2) Contain: quarantine the binary and isolate the host if the hash is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: sweep org-wide for the same hash/filename, then correlate with pipicka.xyz C2 and Run-key persistence on affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LabubaRAT user-level autostart persistence (Run key / scheduled task referencing NVIDIA loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Run/RunOnce registry writes or scheduled-task creation that reference the LabubaRAT loader (nvidia-sysruntime) or its C2 (pipicka.xyz), or that are written by an nvidia-named process — the 'user level autostart' persistence the article says LabubaRAT maintains. Rationale: Article explicitly notes LabubaRAT maintains 'user level autostart'; keying Run-key value data on the named loader and pipicka.xyz IOC keeps this tight while the nvidia-writer clause catches renamed variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine NVIDIA GeForce Experience / driver auto-update writing an nvidia Run entry from \Program Files\NVIDIA
  • Software-deployment tooling staging an nvidia launcher in Run for post-reboot install
  • Backup/imaging solution restoring a legacy Run value
  • Analyst re-adding a known-good nvidia autostart during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Run value data and confirm the referenced binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader (not \Program Files\NVIDIA). 2) Contain: delete the autostart value/task, quarantine the referenced binary, isolate host. 3) Hunt: check for the same value across the fleet and correlate with pipicka.xyz beaconing and loader execution.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or ActingProcessName contains "\\nvidia"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized NVIDIA installer download from non-NVIDIA source AIDelivery Medium
Hunts creation/download of an nvidia-named executable whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is NOT an NVIDIA domain, or that is written to disk by a browser/mail client — the delivery vector for the fake NVIDIA container-runtime installer that drops LabubaRAT. Rationale: The 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise implies a fake installer; keying an nvidia-named exe on a non-NVIDIA origin URL (mark-of-the-web) or a browser/mail-client writer surfaces the delivery without alerting on legitimate NVIDIA downloads. Sigma/Datadog omitted because origin-URL is not a standard field for those log shapes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users downloading NVIDIA drivers from a legitimate mirror/CDN not on the allowlist (e.g. an OEM or Steam-hosted redistributable)
  • Internal software portal re-hosting NVIDIA installers on a corporate URL
  • Driver-management tools (Snappy/Chocolatey) fetching nvidia packages
  • Archived nvidia installer copied from a file share and re-tagged with a referrer URL

| where not(FileOriginUrl has_any ("chocolatey.org","steamstatic.com") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FileOriginUrl + referrer and SHA256; confirm the source domain is attacker-controlled and the file is unsigned/non-NVIDIA. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the source domain at the proxy, and check whether it was executed. 3) Hunt: search EmailUrlInfo/EmailAttachmentInfo for the same lure, and sweep the fleet for the hash plus subsequent nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and pipicka.xyz traffic.

NVIDIA-branded process outbound to non-NVIDIA public infrastructure (LabubaRAT C2 / SOCKS5 proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioral C2 hunt: any nvidia-named process making public network connections to destinations that are NOT NVIDIA infrastructure. Catches LabubaRAT's HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxy traffic even when the operator swaps out pipicka.xyz for fresh infrastructure (the article stresses the binary is re-tasked per campaign). Rationale: Behavioral complement to the pipicka.xyz IOC hunt: legitimate NVIDIA software talks only to NVIDIA/CDN infrastructure, so an nvidia-named process reaching arbitrary public IPs/domains captures LabubaRAT's re-taskable HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxying. Sentinel left blank — this tenant's Sentinel network tables (ImNetworkSession/CommonSecurityLog) don't carry the initiating process image needed to bind the connection to nvidia*.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NVIDIA software contacting a licensing/telemetry endpoint on a non-nvidia.com CDN (Akamai/Cloudflare edge)
  • GeForce Experience pulling game-ready driver assets from a third-party CDN
  • OEM nvidia utility phoning home to the OEM's domain
  • Crash-reporter uploading to a non-NVIDIA error-aggregation service
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the remote IP/domain and check reputation/passive-DNS; confirm the initiating binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader and assess connection periodicity for beaconing. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across the fleet, correlate with pipicka.xyz DNS, Run-key persistence, and loader execution; review for SOCKS5 listener/relay behavior.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "nvidia.com" or RemoteUrl has "nvidia.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith "nvidia.co")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "nvidia.com" or RemoteUrl has "nvidia.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith "nvidia.co")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: NVIDIA-Branded Process Connects to Non-NVIDIA Host (LabubaRAT C2)
id: 5f2b9d84-1c67-4a30-8e91-6b3d7c0e2f88
description: Detects an nvidia-named process initiating a network connection to a destination that is not NVIDIA infrastructure, consistent with LabubaRAT C2 / SOCKS5 proxy traffic.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:

  - attack.t1090
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|contains: '\nvidia'
    Initiated: 'true'
  filter_nvidia:
    DestinationHostname|contains: 'nvidia.com'
  condition: selection and not filter_nvidia
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\nvidia* OR *\NVIDIA*) -@DestinationHostname:*nvidia.com*
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\nvidia.*\.exe$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| iplocation dest
| where isnotnull(dest) AND NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",dest) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",dest)
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process="*nvidia*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| iplocation dest

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("pipicka.xyz")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["pipicka.xyz"]);
ImNetworkSession

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

pip install redirected to non-PyPI index / find-links (dependency confusion) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts pip invocations that pull packages from an --index-url / --extra-index-url / --find-links pointing anywhere other than pypi.org or files.pythonhosted.org. This is the article's 'custom web server / alternate index' hosting-layer abuse used to serve malicious packages or dependency-confusion payloads. Rationale: Anchors on the article's custom-index hosting layer using the exact pip flags (--index-url/--extra-index-url/--find-links) and excludes the two canonical PyPI hosts (pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org) the article names as the legitimate download path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal corporate PyPI mirror (Artifactory/Nexus/devpi) configured via --index-url on the CLI
  • CI/CD build agents installing from a private package feed URL
  • Developers testing a local devpi/pypiserver during package development
  • Air-gapped hosts using --find-links against an offline wheelhouse directory
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the index/find-links host from ProcessCommandLine; is it a known internal mirror or an external/unrecognised domain or raw IP? Check WHOIS/first-seen. 2) Contain: if the host is untrusted, isolate the endpoint, capture the pip cache and any newly created site-packages dirs, and block the domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for child process spawns from the installed package, .pth writes into site-packages, and outbound C2 from python; check whether PIP_INDEX_URL/PIP_CONFIG_FILE was set persistently to make the redirect survive.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or (FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python3","python") and ProcessCommandLine has "pip"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\pip.exe","\\pip3.exe","\\python.exe","\\python3.exe")
| where CommandLine has "install"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pip Install From Non-PyPI Index or Find-Links Source
id: 6b2f9c1a-8d4e-4a7b-9f21-3c7e5a1d0f42
description: Detects pip installing packages from an alternate index URL or find-links location that is not the official PyPI, matching the custom-repository hosting abuse described by Cisco Talos.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains: 'install'
  selection_index:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--index-url'
      - '--extra-index-url'
      - '--find-links'
  filter_official:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'pypi.org'
      - 'files.pythonhosted.org'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flags and selection_index and not filter_official
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\pip.exe OR *\pip3.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\Python.exe) @CommandLine:*install* (@CommandLine:*--index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--extra-index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--find-links*) -(@CommandLine:*pypi.org* OR @CommandLine:*files.pythonhosted.org*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/\binstall\b/i
| CommandLine=/--(index-url|extra-index-url|find-links)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/(pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Python setup.py install-time code execution spawning shell/LOLBin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core sdist build-hook abuse: setup.py executes arbitrary code the moment pip builds/installs a source distribution. Fires when a Python process running setup.py (or its pip parent) spawns a shell, script host, or download LOLBin. Rationale: Uses the article's central claim that setup.py 'executes automatically during installation, allowing for the execution of arbitrary code' — pivoting on the setup.py parent command line spawning a shell/download LOLBin. Falcon variant approximates via python/pip parent because FDR ProcessRollup2 does not expose parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit packages with C/C++ extensions whose setup.py shells out to a compiler wrapper or configure script during build
  • setup.py calling git.exe/curl to fetch version metadata or submodules at build time
  • Developer running 'python setup.py test' that invokes a shell-based test harness
  • Vendored build scripts that call certutil/bitsadmin for legitimate artifact retrieval on locked-down build agents
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl.exe","gcc","clang","cmake","configure","vcvars"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the package name/path from InitiatingProcessCommandLine; decode any base64/encoded payload and identify the package being installed. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the sdist tarball + pip cache; pull the package from the resolved index and preserve setup.py. 3) Hunt: check other hosts that installed the same package name/version, look for .pth persistence written into site-packages, credential-file reads, and outbound connections from the python process during the install window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious .pth file dropped into site-packages by pip/python AIInstallation Medium
Hunts install-time persistence via a .pth file written into site-packages/dist-packages. Python auto-executes any line in a .pth file beginning with 'import' on every interpreter start, giving transient-to-persistent code execution — the TeamPCP litellm_init.pth technique that aligns with the article's persistent build-hook abuse. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'Persistent' build-hook abuse row (setup.py+pyproject.toml, sdist+wheel) and corroborated by TeamPCP's litellm_init.pth in-package persistence; the site-packages/dist-packages path plus a .pth extension written by pip/python is the exact drop location, with the two standard tooling .pth files excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editable installs (pip install -e .) dropping __editable__.<pkg>.pth or setuptools' generated .pth
  • Packages like matplotlib/pywin32/virtualenv legitimately shipping a .pth to extend sys.path
  • conda/virtualenv creation writing standard path-configuration .pth files
  • IDE (PyCharm/VS Code) creating a project .pth for interpreter path management
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName startswith "__editable__" or FileName in~ ("__editable___finder.pth","virtualenv.pth","pywin32.pth"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .pth contents — a benign one contains only directory paths; flag any line starting with 'import' or containing exec/eval/base64. 2) Contain: if it executes code, isolate the host, delete/quarantine the .pth, and identify the parent package from the surrounding .dist-info. 3) Hunt: enumerate all interpreters on the host for the same .pth, sweep other endpoints that installed the same package/version, and correlate to any non-PyPI index redirect (UC1) or setup.py execution (UC2) in the same install window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".pth"
| where FolderPath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(FileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(TargetFileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Persistent PIP_ index/config environment variable set in registry AIInstallation High
Alerts when a PIP_INDEX_URL / PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL / PIP_FIND_LINKS / PIP_CONFIG_FILE environment variable is written to the user or system Environment registry key. Per the article, any pip CLI arg converts to a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var — persisting one silently redirects ALL future pip installs to attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Directly operationalises the article's statement that any pip argument becomes a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var (naming PIP_CONFIG_FILE and PIP_FIND_LINKS) — writing these under the Environment registry key is a low-FP, high-fidelity redirect/persistence primitive. Falcon left empty: FDR does not reliably ship Session Manager\Environment writes as an AsepValueUpdate event. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1112 T1574.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer permanently pointing pip at a corporate mirror by setting PIP_INDEX_URL in user environment
  • IT provisioning script/GPO that pushes PIP_CONFIG_FILE to a managed pip.ini for all developers
  • CI runner bootstrap that exports PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL for a private feed
  • DevOps setting PIP_TARGET/PIP_PREFIX for a shared build environment
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — is the URL/config path an approved internal mirror or an external/unknown host? Identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and whether it was interactive or scripted. 2) Contain: if untrusted, delete the value, block the destination at the proxy, and audit any pip installs that ran after the value was set. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (non-PyPI index installs) and UC2/UC3 on the same host and any host sharing the GPO/provisioning source; verify no pip.ini/pip.conf on disk was also modified to the same destination.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValue in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

Miasma/AsyncAPI first-stage: node spawns detached 'node -e' downloader referencing IPFS/sync.js AIDelivery High
Hunts the AsyncAPI supply-chain first stage: a Node process spawns a detached child `node -e '<obfuscated>'` whose inline string table carries the plaintext IPFS gateway URL, the stage-2 CID, and the drop filename sync.js. Fires on package-import-triggered download rather than any npm lifecycle hook. Rationale: Anchored on verbatim strings from the shipped downloader string table (both IPFS CIDs, the ipfs.io gateway path, drop name sync.js) combined with the node->node -e detached-spawn shape. CIDs and the download-to-per-user-dir behaviour are confirmed by Wiz and SafeDep, so a require()-triggered node -e hit on these is unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scripting an IPFS pin/fetch with `node -e` against ipfs.io during dApp/Web3 work
  • CI job that inlines a node -e helper referencing a file literally named sync.js (rare)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • Internal reproduction/IR testing of this exact payload after the advisory
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and confirm it contains an ipfs.io CID and sync.js; check the parent node process's working dir / project for an installed @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2(-alpha.1), @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1 or generator-components@0.7.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node child, and quarantine %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js (or ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to 85.137.53.71 and for ~/.config/.miasma/ artifacts and miasma-monitor persistence; rotate any npm/GitHub/AWS tokens and SSH keys exposed on that host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Miasma stage-2 dropped: sync.js written to per-user NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage loader landing on disk. The downloader writes the encrypted IPFS object as sync.js into the per-user Node data dir (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS on macOS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS on Linux), written by a node process. Rationale: The drop filename (sync.js) and the exact per-user NodeJS data directories are stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by SafeDep/Wiz as the stage-2 write location. A node-written sync.js in that dir has effectively no benign meaning — Node itself never creates that file there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated Node tooling that coincidentally creates a cache file named sync.js under an app dir containing the token 'NodeJS' (uncommon)
  • EDR replay/rehydration of a quarantined sample regenerating the file
  • IR/forensic copy of the artifact onto a monitored analyst workstation
  • Backup/sync agent restoring an infected user profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare against known stage-2 loaders (~8.24-8.25 MB); confirm the writing process is node and identify the parent project with an affected @asyncapi package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, kill any node process executing it, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for outbound to 85.137.53.71, for ~/.config/.miasma/ identity/lock files and miasma-monitor persistence, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same @asyncapi versions in the compromise window.

Miasma stage-2 executed: node runs sync.js from NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the dropped loader — a node process launched with a command line pointing at sync.js inside the per-user NodeJS data directory. This is the detached persistence/loader run that decrypts and evaluates the M-RED-TEAM stage-3 implant. Rationale: Distinct pivot from the first stage: instead of an inline node -e, this catches node executing the on-disk sync.js by path (NodeJS dir + sync.js), the stage-2 loader run. Path and filename are article-verbatim and corroborated as the loader location. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/

1) Triage: capture full ProcessCommandLine and the sync.js path/hash; confirm the parent is a detached node (unref'd) and not an interactive dev session. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, quarantine sync.js. 3) Hunt: look for the resulting HTTP C2 to 85.137.53.71 (three ports), for miasma-monitor persistence and ~/.config/.miasma/ paths, and sweep the fleet for the same loader path; force credential rotation on the affected account.

Miasma M-RED-TEAM HTTP C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host contacting the confirmed Miasma/M-RED-TEAM HTTP C2 endpoint 85.137.53.71 (operated on three ports). This is the stage-3 implant's primary command-and-control channel and a hard network IOC. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is a dedicated Miasma HTTP C2 host independently confirmed by Wiz, SafeDep, and The Hacker News (three ports). A hard-IOC network match with near-zero benign traffic; projecting the initiating process/port surfaces the beaconing binary and channel for triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/scanning appliance or a SOC honeypot deliberately probing the C2 IP
  • Sandbox detonation egressing to the live C2
  • Researcher curl/browser test against the IP from a corporate host
  • Shared-egress NAT causing a benign-looking source if the true infected host isn't attributed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node) and the destination port; confirm the host installed an affected @asyncapi version and has %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 at the egress/firewall, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing node process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the sync.js drop/exec and the node -e downloader on the same host, sweep all egress logs for other hosts hitting the IP, and rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials that were reachable from the compromised host.

| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
